examples.name: Primary action with closely related alternatives
examples.description: The common case - a labeled primary action plus a small group of alternatives reachable from the caret segment.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  secondaryActionLabel="More save options"
  sections={[
    {
      id: 'save-options',
      items: [
        { id: 'save-as', label: 'Save as...', onSelect: () => saveAs() },
        { id: 'save-copy', label: 'Save a copy', onSelect: () => saveCopy() },
      ],
    },
  ]}
  onClick={() => save()}
>
  Save
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Primary appearance
examples.description: appearance applies uniformly to both segments, matching every verified Figma variant.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  appearance="primary"
  secondaryActionLabel="More send options"
  sections={sendAlternatives}
  onClick={() => sendForSignature()}
>
  Send for signature
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense toolbar
examples.description: size applies uniformly to both segments, matching Button's own four sizes exactly.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton size="sm" secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Loading primary action
examples.description: isLoading applies Button's own loading treatment to the primary action and also disables the secondary action - picking an alternative while the primary action is mid-flight would be confusing.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton isLoading secondaryActionLabel="More save options" sections={saveAlternatives} onClick={() => save()}>
  Saving...
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Disabling both segments together
examples.description: disabled disables both segments together (native disabled on both), matching how Figma's own isDisabled axis covers the whole component, not one segment.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton disabled secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Forwarding other Button props
examples.description: Every other ButtonProps prop (tone, iconBefore, iconAfter, any native button attribute) forwards straight to the primary action via {...rest}.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  tone="warning"
  iconBefore={<AlertIcon decorative />}
  secondaryActionLabel="More options"
  sections={alternatives}
  onClick={() => flagForReview()}
>
  Flag for review
</SplitButton>

antiExamples.name: Using Split Button for a single action with no alternatives
antiExamples.reason: sections is meant for a small group of closely related alternatives, not an empty placeholder - a single action with no alternatives should use Button directly instead of carrying an unused caret segment.

antiExamples.name: Expecting an auto-derived secondary action label
antiExamples.reason: secondaryActionLabel is required, not derived from children - the caret segment has no visible text of its own to derive an accessible name from. TypeScript rejects this at compile time.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a 'subtle' appearance
antiExamples.jsx:
<SplitButton appearance="subtle" secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>
antiExamples.reason: appearance is deliberately narrower than Button's own ('default' | 'primary' only) - Figma never shows a subtle split button, so code doesn't invent one. TypeScript rejects this at compile time.
